why: Shorter: drops the redundant Finnish-window answer sentence before the guess (cut low-value sentences, shorter wins) and the guess prompt comes right after the setup; also 'before you watch the second session run' referred to something not on the slide.
'one run at a time' matches the agent-run vocabulary and is a plain word; 'session' is a poor word per the author's own call (tn-on-your-side), though the difference is small.
Closing sentence 'The kit you grow on your own is the one that counts' adds little and is a kicker; author cuts such closers (calls page 2026-11-01, shorter wins).
'YOUR real work is the material' vs 'The training runs on YOUR real work' are equivalent in length and claim; and B arguably opens on a description of the course, but no clear rule favours either.
Shorter: it merges two sentences into one and drops the 'It often isn't.' beat, following 'the shorter version wins when the difference is a removed sentence or clause'.
Drops the count, following 'a count becomes a frame the student controls when the number does no memory work'. The three bullets already show how many there are.
Author's own call: the cut clause 'catches the branches you can't see' adds real why-information, pointing at unknown unknowns.
Shorter, fewer words read faster; B adds extra clauses, an em-dash aside, and a narrator-style explanation of the reversals. A drops the hedgy asides.

B names the claim (recurring work has a shape, easier to recognise drawn); A's 'forest before the trees' is a stock metaphor the training never builds, which the taste rules reject, though B is wordier.

B opens on a concrete action the student can take (Ask for a ranked list), per 'open on what the student does' and 'concrete action beats framework'; A's essay-title is a witty kicker describing the machine.
B coins 'the wall', an invented concept (taste-notes: 'The wall is not a thing/concept in the industry'); A makes the same point in plain words.
Past call tn-read-the-shapes: cutting 'Claude proposes' from the title means fewer words, which read faster.
B adds a closing sentence ('places, not a pipeline') that restates the point; per the author's cuts, a low-value closer goes and shorter wins.
A keeps 'Module 3 draws that boundary for your own repo', which the author rejected as an unintelligible abstraction and a forward hint; B cuts it.
B adds 'The contrast is the lesson/material' restating a point already made; cut-the-restatement call (M4 'contrast is the lesson' cut), shorter wins.
A's 'not typing markdown' restatement and 'reasons land in Phase 3' forward hint are low-value sentences the author cuts (forward hints, restatements); shorter wins.
Shorter wins: B cuts the redundant restated lead-in and the 'a result you can read is enough' sentence, which duplicates the next line's point (cut low-value restatements).
Only bold markup differs; the wording is identical, so no taste rule favours either.
